newsitem.title: USA: Citicorp Q1 gives mixed picture.
newsitem.headline: Citicorp Q1 gives mixed picture.

text.p: Citicorp's first-quarter 1997 earnings reflected a "relatively weak" consumer business and a "relatively strong" corporate banking business, Thomas Jones, executive vice president and principal financial officer told analysts Tuesday.

Overall, Citicorp earlier Tuesday reported net income rose nine percent from a year ago to $995 million from a year ago and, reflecting fewer shares outstanding, earnings per share fully diluted rose 15 percent to $2.01 from $1.75.
In a statement with the earnings, chairman John Reed said the earnings were "on track."

Referring to the U.S. credit card business, where Citicorp is the largest issuer and loss rates have been creeping up throughout the industry, Jones said: "We are growing this portfolio as much as we want do.
"It doesn't take a genius to know that this is a benign economy and all recoveries one day end."
He addedthat "on the whole. we feel pretty well positioned."
In the fourth quarter, Citicorp's U.S. credit card loss rate rose to 5.91 percent from 5.45 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 and 4.38 percent in the first quarter of 1996.
Jones said that in the U.S., card portfolio, bankruptcies and 30-day and 90-day delinquencies rates all remained "fairly stable."
In the card business worldwide, Citicorp had first-quarter net income of $224 million, down 14 percent from the first quarter of 1996.

According to a Citicorp chart, the "lagged net credit loss rate" which shows current U.S. card charge-offs against volume 12 months ago was 6.21 percent in the 1997 first quarter. The loss rate stated by most issuers in earnings reports shows the current charge-offs against the current volume.

Although the 12-month lagged ratio figure is about 30 basis points higher than the current or "coincidental" rate, Jones said the lagged rate compares quite favorably to certain competitors who are growing their card receivables rapidly.
Jones declined to give a prediction on when credit card loss rates might stop rising in the U.S. He added that, for Citicorp, "the rate of increase is not dramatic."
He also said he is confident "there isn't any big hole" lurking in the future.

In response to a question about how Citicorp might participate in the current wave of consolidation in the U.S. financial services industry, Jones said any deal would have to enhance shareholder value.
Areas of interest include investment management and insurance and also acquisitions overseas where many emerging economies are growing faster than in the U.S.

In response to a question at a subsequent session with reporters, Jones said Citicorp is "prepared for" currency convergence in Europe and, while it reduces foreign exchange volatility, it "may even be a positive" in other ways.
